headline: Earlier today, the Iraqi Armed Forces shot down an unidentified unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) in the Muwailihah area, north of Babylon Governorate, southern Iraq. There is considerable speculation regarding the UAV's identity, with some suggesting it could be a Chinese-made CH-4B or Wing Loong II operated by the Royal Saudi Air Force (RSAF). However, the wreckage appears to show a 4-blade composite pusher propeller, whereas both the CH-4B and Wing Loong II are equipped with 3-blade pusher propellers. Based on that detail, those two platforms seem unlikely. The only UAVs that come to mind with a 4-blade pusher propeller are the MQ-9B (SkyGuardian/SeaGuardian) and the MQ-9A Extended Range (ER). The standard MQ-9A (Block 1/Block 5) uses a 3-blade propeller.

headline: If that didn't happen in the last war, when Iran was launching an average of 40 ballistic missiles per day for weeks, how do you expect to do it now, especially after massively depleting your JASSM stockpile? People need to stay grounded in reality. There's a reason Trump ended the campaign two days ago instead of continuing it: it simply wasn't sustainable. You can't keep pounding Iran indefinitely while seeing no meaningful results. Iran isn't winning or losing. It's simply forcing the United States to burn through its munitions. The targeted bases are still operational, damaged entrances can be repaired within hours, and after 40 days of fighting, they destroyed only around three launchers (documented). Iranian launchers are also relatively easy to build since they rely on hydraulic systems. On top of that, no actual evidence has been presented showing that Iran's ballistic missile production was significantly degraded. In fact, both Iranian officials and U.S. media have since reported that production not only continues but has accelerated since the war. Meanwhile, according to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the United States expended between 3,710 and 4,510 key precision-guided munitions during the Iran War, equivalent to roughly 31–38% of its estimated pre-war stockpile. Air defense interceptors saw the steepest depletion, with an estimated 190–290 of 360 THAAD interceptors expended (up to 80%), 130–250 of 410 SM-3 interceptors (more than half), and 1,060–1,430 of 2,330 Patriot interceptors (up to 61%). Long-range strike weapons were also heavily consumed. The analysis estimates the U.S. fired more than 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles, over 1,100 JASSM air-launched cruise missiles, and 40–70 of its estimated 90 Precision Strike Missiles (PrSMs), leaving the relatively new missile with a significantly reduced inventory. Replenishing some of the most heavily used weapons could take years. No matter how much damage is inflicted on Iranian infrastructure, whether civilian or military, repairs are relatively quick and inexpensive. If this continues, the situation could eventually shift, because the day Iran fields a capable air force, the United States and Israel won't be able to operate as freely as they do today. During the last conflict, IRGC Aerospace Force missile units had enough freedom of action to carry out what was effectively a counter-force campaign against high-value U.S. targets at ranges exceeding 1,000 km.

headline: RT by @sentdefender: Belgian authorities have arrested a woman who was interning at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) in Mons, Belgium, on suspicion of espionage. The woman, a Canadian citizen of Chinese origin, was detained on Friday, and the Belgian Federal Public Prosecutor's Office announced the arrest on Saturday. Prosecutors suspect that she was spying for a third country and was a member of a criminal organization. Investigators conducted searches at both her home and her workplace at SHAPE. The investigation began when SHAPE's own security services flagged her conduct and reported their concerns to Belgian military intelligence, which subsequently referred the matter to federal prosecutors. SHAPE is NATO's primary military command in Europe, led by the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, and plays a central role in the alliance's operational planning. A SHAPE spokesperson stated that there is no indication that NATO's or SHAPE's operational readiness, command and control arrangements, or ongoing tasks have been affected, confirming that the headquarters continues to operate normally. Authorities have provided few additional details about the case. They have not publicly identified the woman or disclosed the country for which she allegedly spied. This arrest comes amid heightened concerns across Europe regarding foreign intelligence activities targeting NATO institutions and member states. Source: AP, Bloomberg, Washington Post, CBC, Global News. So What The identity of the sponsoring state has not been confirmed. While reports emphasize her Chinese origin, it’s important to note that origin alone is not evidence, and prosecutors have not named anyone specific. It's unlikely that a single intern represents the entire picture; additional handlers or a broader network may be involved. SHAPE, which is NATO's primary military command, is a probable target for any capable hostile service. Although she is individually accused of betraying her country, placing a source within a headquarters like this is standard tradecraft for hostile states, not an exception. According to Reuters, a U.S. official said military commanders advised Trump that the operation had reached the limit of its effectiveness, citing a dwindling target set and concerns from Joint Chiefs Chairman General Dan Caine over declining air defense interceptor stockpiles. Reuters also reports Iran has pledged to suspend attacks as long as the U.S. pause continues, while denying it is returning to the negotiating table. Iranian state media also claimed that six commercial vessels were turned back after attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian permission, underscoring Tehran's insistence that it still controls traffic through the waterway. Source: https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/iran-says-it-still-controls-strait-not-seeking-talks-after-trump-halts-bombing-2026-07-27/

headline: The Wall Street Journal reports that concerns over dwindling U.S. air defense interceptor stockpiles have become a key factor in the administration's decision to pause a major escalation against Iran. According to the Journal, Joint Chiefs Chairman General Dan Caine warned the White House that declining inventories of Patriot and other interceptors would increase the risk to U.S. forces if large scale operations resumed. The report also says the White House sought to prevent publication of updated government figures on Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Air Defense (THAAD) interceptor expenditures, arguing their release could harm national security. President Donald J. Trump disputed reports of a munitions shortfall, telling the Journal the U.S. has "far more munitions than we need." Outside analysts, however, have warned that the high rate of interceptor use in the conflict could strain U.S. air defense capacity and affect readiness for other potential contingencies. Source: https://www.wsj.com/world/middle-east/trump-pauses-iran-strikes-as-officials-weigh-dwindling-air-defense-stocks-c7d7ebb0?st=5u3r67
